Limitations
Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in
Appendix L but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated. We cover 4B–8B scale;
whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closedsource APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples. We do not train a verifier, leaving unknown how much oracle headroom
a supervised approach could recover.
We evaluate at N =8 (primary) and N =16; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix R). The free-form ablation covers SciERC
NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE freeform results are in Appendix L. Qwen3-8B’s SciERC checkpoint used empty <think></think>
blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix I). LP compression worsens on
easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied
fractions reach 95.8% at T =0.7); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested. We tested verbalized confidence
(Tian et al., 2023) as a second per-sample signal;
it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10
on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the
weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix U). Ad-hoc LP×VC combinations yield at
most +0.2 pp over greedy (not significant; §5);
whether learned combinations could close the gap
remains open. The ε=0.05 threshold used for
tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across
ε ∈ [0, 0.2] (Appendix J), the specific subset gains
should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection
strategy. We tested one remedy for LP compression
(entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC (4×);
LP×VC combinations also fail to recover selection
(§5); calibration-based approaches remain unexplored. Our selection experiments use 2 training
seeds (stability σ≤0.026); while within-seed statistical power is high (n=32,565 for Few-NERD),
training seed stochasticity is not exhaustively quantified. Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs
(vs. 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence;
a 5-epoch control experiment is provided in Appendix Z to verify that degeneracy differences are
not training-induced.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection, and the gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\%) collapses the candidate pool; and LP, the sole per-sample signal, requires two jointly necessary conditions: low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
LP selection succeeds when both conditions are met: at 13.8\% degeneracy with strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$; Few-NERD), LP achieves $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 17.8\% with weak alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.24$; SciERC), $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$); at 47.4\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
In the low-degeneracy regime, LP selection scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals cannot close the oracle gap; the bottleneck lies in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation, not in the combination method.
Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open.
Closing the gap for structural signals requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; LP provides a lightweight baseline when both degeneracy and alignment conditions are met.

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
4	All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL), with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}).
5	For selection, LP achieves significant gains only when both conditions are met ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
6	RE signal rankings are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
7	
8	\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
9	Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
10	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) and closes 23--41\% of the oracle gap, but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 47.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
11	Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}); cross-model evidence (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 47.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}) reinforces the pattern.
12	LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$.
13	
14	\paragraph{Non-tied subset and $N$-scaling.}
15	Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, survives Bonferroni; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
16	LP scales with $N$ in the low-degeneracy regime ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16 on Few-NERD, $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}); on SciERC, even $N{=}32$ captures less than 5\% of headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
17	An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (full analyses in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
18	
19	\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
20	Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute: token-level averaging, schema-dominated tokens, vocabulary restriction under constrained decoding, and format-token dilution.
21	Free-form decoding rules out constraint-imposed mechanisms for NER (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) but restores LP selection for RE ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
22	Entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse ($-2.0$~pp SciERC, $-3.3$~pp CoNLL): fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities at the representation level, and compression cannot be broken by disaggregating to entity tokens.
23	LP failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic failure mode.
24	
25	\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
26	At the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17), QE signals collapse (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); at the ceiling boundary (CoNLL, degeneracy 47--89\%), LP fails entirely.
27	In the moderate regime, two conditions jointly determine effectiveness: the cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ fail, 18\% $\to$ weak, 14\% $\to$ strong) is confirmed at entity-type level ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
28	Two independent manipulations (LoRA rank 8: degeneracy 7.2\%, $\rho{=}0.24$; $T{=}1.2$: degeneracy 12.5\%, $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) confirm alignment is largely task-determined; degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.
29	
30	\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
31	Practitioners should first estimate instance degeneracy on a labeled subset (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): in the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%), prefer greedy decoding; structural signals still support quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$).
32	In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%) with adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), LP selection is effective and scales with $N$ ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD; $+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16).
33	Temperature provides a controllable lever for degeneracy (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) but cannot address alignment; training convergence offers a second lever (Few-NERD degeneracy rises from 11\% to 31\% between 3 and 5 epochs, halving LP gains; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}).
34	Standard calibration methods preserve within-instance argmax and cannot change selection; even multi-feature variants yield no improvement ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}), confirming the bottleneck is alignment rather than miscalibration.
35	
36	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL), with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}).
For selection, LP achieves significant gains only when both conditions are met ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
RE signal rankings are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) and closes 23--41\% of the oracle gap, but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 47.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}); cross-model evidence (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 47.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}) reinforces the pattern.
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset and $N$-scaling.}
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, survives Bonferroni; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
LP scales with $N$ in the low-degeneracy regime ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16 on Few-NERD, $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}); on SciERC, even $N{=}32$ captures less than 5\% of headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (full analyses in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute: token-level averaging, schema-dominated tokens, vocabulary restriction under constrained decoding, and format-token dilution.
Free-form decoding rules out constraint-imposed mechanisms for NER (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) but restores LP selection for RE ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
Entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse ($-2.0$~pp SciERC, $-3.3$~pp CoNLL): fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities at the representation level, and compression cannot be broken by disaggregating to entity tokens.
LP failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic failure mode.

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
At the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17), QE signals collapse (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); at the ceiling boundary (CoNLL, degeneracy 47--89\%), LP fails entirely.
In the moderate regime, two conditions jointly determine effectiveness: the cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ fail, 18\% $\to$ weak, 14\% $\to$ strong) is confirmed at entity-type level ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
Two independent manipulations (LoRA rank 8: degeneracy 7.2\%, $\rho{=}0.24$; $T{=}1.2$: degeneracy 12.5\%, $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) confirm alignment is largely task-determined; degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.

\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
Practitioners should first estimate instance degeneracy on a labeled subset (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): in the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%), prefer greedy decoding; structural signals still support quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$).
In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%) with adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), LP selection is effective and scales with $N$ ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD; $+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16).
Temperature provides a controllable lever for degeneracy (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) but cannot address alignment; training convergence offers a second lever (Few-NERD degeneracy rises from 11\% to 31\% between 3 and 5 epochs, halving LP gains; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}).
Standard calibration methods preserve within-instance argmax and cannot change selection; even multi-feature variants yield no improvement ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}), confirming the bottleneck is alignment rather than miscalibration.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; even supervised combination of all five signals fails to close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Effective selection requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N{=}8$ captures most QE benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation fails to yield selection improvements, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A methodological premise structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that by design assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	These signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
13	Yet quality estimation does not translate to structural selection, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (the disparity between a signal's ability to rank instances reliably and its failure to select the best output within a single instance): structural best-of-$N$ selection matches or degrades greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 12\textendash 14~pp oracle headroom.

33	    A three-layer failure: instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR fails because degeneracy (14\textendash 47\%) collapses the candidate pool; LP requires both low degeneracy and adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
